raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 60-year-old man, presented with fever, chills, and sweats, followed by an altered level of consciousness with a Glasgow coma scale score at 3. He had returned 18 days earlier from a trip to India and underwent a transrectal ultrasound guided prostate biopsy with ciprofloxacin antibiotic prophylaxis the day before. The patient was then sedated, intubated, and admitted to intensive care. The pupils were equal and he had no nuchal rigidity. Initial laboratory examination of peripheral blood showed: haemoglobin 158 g/L, white blood cell count (WBC) 13 x 109 cells/L (neutrophils 90%), platelet count 80 x 109 cells/L, AST 605 IU/L, ALT 355 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, INR 3.12, serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, serum urea 28 mg/dL.
Management consisted in invasive mechanical ventilation, norepinephrine infusion, and anti-infective treatment with cefotaxime, amoxicillin, and aciclovir, quickly replaced by meropenem, fosfomycin, and amikacin following the discovery of a multidrug-resistant Escherichia Coli on blood cultures.
Despite stopping the sedative infusions and a normal brain CT scan, there was no change in the level of consciousness. Furthermore, peripheral blood analysis demonstrated rapidly deteriorating acute kidney and liver failure:haemoglobin 110 g/L, white blood cell count (WBC) 15 x 109 cells/L (neutrophils 90%), platelet count 17 x 109 cells/L, AST 17000 IU/L, ALT 9500 IU/L, total bilirubin 4.7 mg/dL, INR 6.76, serum creatinine 4.5 mg/dL, serum urea 36 mg/dL.
A liver screen including serological testing for hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) was negative. Serum paracetamol concentration was less than 1 mg/L. Ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, ferritin and an autoimmune screen were all negative. Dengue and other arbovirus infections were ruled out, and thick blood films were negative for malaria parasites. The initial leptospirosis serology (ELISA and MAT) was negative. Abdominal ultrasound did not demonstrate any vascular cause.
Renal replacement therapy with CVVH and hepatoprotection (N-acetylcysteine) were initiated. Finally, a highly urgent orthotopic liver transplantation was performed for fulminant hepatic failure, 6 days after the initial appearance of symptoms.
Following liver transplantation and cessation of sedation, whilst liver function tests and serum ammonia level returned to normal, an altered level of consciousness persisted which was associated with cerebellar ataxia, facial dyskinesia, swallowing disorders, and tremulousness of hands. Electroencephalography, cranial magnetic resonance imaging, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis (no cells; normal glucose and proteins) were unremarkable. The diagnosis of leptospirosis with fulminant hepatitis failure and neuro-leptospirosis was finally made in view of the positivity of leptospira serology (ELISA and MAT) 2 weeks after the onset of symptoms. An Indian strain of Leptospira Hebdomadis was identified. The interrogation taught us later that the patient was led into a river whilst on an elephant ride, 3 days before his return to France. PCR performed 25 days after admission did not detect Leptospira DNA in the blood, CSF, or urine.
The clinical evolution was finally favourable, with progressive disappearance of cerebellar ataxia and improved renal function after several weeks. The patient was discharged to return home 74 days after the onset of symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male presenting with fever, chills, sweats, and acute coma with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 3.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A previously healthy 60-year-old male presented with acute fever, chills, and sweats followed by rapid neurological collapse to a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 3. He had returned 18 days prior from India and had undergone a transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy under ciprofloxacin prophylaxis the day before presentation. He was sedated, intubated, and admitted to the ICU on mechanical ventilation and vasopressors. Despite clearance of sedation and initial antimicrobial escalation, consciousness remained depressed, and he developed fulminant hepatic and renal failure. Following emergency orthotopic liver transplantation on day 6 post-onset, hepatic parameters normalized, but neurological deficits (cerebellar ataxia, facial dyskinesia, dysphagia, and tremors) persisted for several weeks before gradually improving until discharge on day 74.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Underwent transrectal ultrasound-guided prostate biopsy with oral ciprofloxacin prophylaxis 1 day prior to admission. Epidemiological exposure: Returned 18 days prior from a trip to India, during which he was exposed to river water during an elephant ride 3 days prior to returning to France.

objective.physical_examination: Upon presentation: GCS 3, pupils equal and reactive, no nuchal rigidity. Hemodynamically unstable requiring norepinephrine infusion. Post-liver transplantation examination revealed persistent impaired consciousness, cerebellar ataxia, facial dyskinesia, swallowing disorders, and coarse hand tremors.
objective.routine_investigations:
Initial ICU presentation: Hemoglobin 158 g/L, WBC 13 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 90%), platelet count 80 x 10^9 cells/L, AST 605 IU/L, ALT 355 IU/L, total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, INR 3.12, serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, serum urea 28 mg/dL.
Pre-transplant deterioration: Hemoglobin 110 g/L, WBC 15 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 90%), platelet count 17 x 10^9 cells/L, AST 17,000 IU/L, ALT 9,500 IU/L, total bilirubin 4.7 mg/dL, INR 6.76, serum creatinine 4.5 mg/dL, serum urea 36 mg/dL.
Routine/differential workup: Hepatitis A, B, C, HIV, HSV, CMV, and EBV panels negative; serum paracetamol <1 mg/L; ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, ferritin, and autoimmune screen negative; dengue and arbovirus tests negative; thick blood smears negative for Plasmodium (malaria). Blood cultures grew multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli.
objective.advanced_workup:
Brain CT: Normal.
Abdominal ultrasound: No vascular thrombosis or vascular cause for liver failure.
Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: Acellular, normal glucose and normal protein.
Cranial MRI: Unremarkable.
Electroencephalography: Unremarkable.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed leptospirosis complicated by fulminant hepatic failure and neuroleptospirosis (cerebellar ataxia, dyskinesia, encephalopathy), with secondary multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli bacteremia post-prostate biopsy. Initial acute-phase serology (ELISA and MAT) on presentation was negative, but repeat serology at 2 weeks post-onset was positive, identifying an Indian strain of Leptospira Hebdomadis. Late PCR at day 25 post-admission was negative in blood, CSF, and urine. Differentials of viral hepatitis, acetaminophen toxicity, malaria, arboviruses, and structural CNS lesions were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Initial anti-infectives (cefotaxime, amoxicillin, acyclovir) were switched to meropenem, fosfomycin, and amikacin for MDR E. coli bacteremia. Supported with invasive mechanical ventilation, norepinephrine, CVVH, N-acetylcysteine, and emergency orthotopic liver transplantation 6 days post-onset. Neurological deficits and renal dysfunction gradually resolved over several weeks, leading to successful home discharge 74 days after symptom onset.
